one_line: Gastroenterologist who joined SCPMG in 1969, led it as executive medical director for ten years, and still practices.
top_role: Executive Medical Director, Southern California Permanente Medical Group

excluded_segments.reason: Narrator asked to go off the record: "another aspect this this is off the tape now isn't it, Paul. We're not I mean." (interviewer: "We can stop the recording.")

journey.label: Army medical unit sparks medicine
journey.fortune_basis: I thought, gee, this being a doctor is a terrific idea
journey.quote: they took a fondness to me and would ask me, what do you want to do? And I thought, gee, this being a doctor is a terrific idea.

journey.year_note: He says his UCLA/VA training ended 'about 1968' and he then briefly went to Cedars before joining KP in July 1969.
journey.label: Tries private practice, dislikes it
journey.fortune_basis: didn't like anything about private practice
journey.quote: Uh, ending that in about 1968. I briefly went to Cedars to become a practicing gastroenterologist and didn't like anything about private practice.

journey.label: Joins SCPMG at Los Angeles
journey.fortune_basis: invited me to join the department at Los Angeles Medical Center
journey.quote: friends at Kaiser Permanente who, uh, invited me to join the department at Los Angeles Medical Center in July 1969.

journey.label: Speaks up, trains nurse practitioners
journey.fortune_basis: Oliver, you were right on. We like you here.
journey.quote: The medical director said, Oliver, you were right on. We like you here. And that led to being offered an opportunity to train the nurse practitioners.

journey.label: Physician liaison to leadership program
journey.fortune_basis: learned a lot about physician management
journey.quote: asked to be, uh, the physician liaison to the Middle Management Leadership Development Program by Dr. Murray, our medical director.

journey.label: Runs for EMD, loses
journey.fortune_basis: I won the popular vote, actually, but the board correctly decided Dr. Murray was preferred
journey.quote: in 1979, I was an elected member to the board, and I was the assistant medical director, assistant chief of medicine at our tertiary medical center. And I ran for a executive medical director

journey.year_note: He turned down the regional post Dr. Murray offered 'at that time, 1979', then transferred to West LA.
journey.label: Becomes West LA chief of medicine
journey.fortune_basis: The department was in trouble. Very unusual to transfer medical centers
journey.quote: And so I turned that down, transferred to West LA as Chief of Internal Medicine. The department was in trouble. Very unusual to transfer medical centers

journey.year_note: He says "in 1994, I became the medical director" (52:30) and "1994 to 2004" four more times. Once, at 7:08, just before this quote, he says "10 years later, in 1989"; the clip starts after that line.
journey.label: Elected executive medical director
journey.fortune_basis: I think well liked and well respected and quite, quite ambitious
journey.quote: I was by that time well known in the medical group and I think well liked and well respected and quite, quite ambitious.

journey.year_note: He describes this as happening when he came into office as executive medical director, which he dates to 1994 elsewhere.
journey.label: Rejects plan to merge management
journey.fortune_basis: That was a personal challenge. Worked out okay.
journey.quote: This, this is off the table. I don't even know anything about this. Do you people realize I'm new? I'm the new executive. That was a personal challenge.

journey.label: Health plan loses hundreds of millions
journey.quote: Then the financial crisis came when we began to lose hundreds of millions of dollars

journey.label: Backs failed cardiac surgery move
journey.quote: I endorsed it, I announced it, I publicly supported it. I that was the mistake. Okay. The whole thing was built on stilts. It was stupid, okay? And it failed immediately.

journey.label: Re-elected despite admitted error
journey.fortune_basis: Notwithstanding that error in my thinking process, I'm proud of that.
journey.quote: I made a mistake in supporting closing some Kaiser hospitals. It was a mistake. Error. I was reelected two years after that by the medical group.

journey.label: Pitches Las Vegas expansion, rebuffed
journey.fortune_basis: So I went back to our health plan, they were not interested in it.
journey.quote: I remember going to Las Vegas in 1997, sitting in some dark restaurant Italian restaurant with a glass of wine with some fellow who owned the health plan there, and I said, we want it.

journey.label: Launches patient ratings of physicians
journey.fortune_basis: Which I'm proud of. I'm very proud of that
journey.quote: Let's do maps. And since then, 1999, maybe 2000, we assess our physicians by membership, uh, assessments.

journey.label: Helps unite medical groups in Federation
journey.fortune_basis: I was most proud of taking the lead on bringing the Permanente Medical Groups together
journey.quote: I was most proud of taking the lead on bringing the Permanente Medical Groups together in the Federation. Not the single leader but bringing us together as a more singular force.

journey.year_note: He says he is 87 and still working at the time of the interview, recorded 2026-02-04.
journey.label: Longest-tenured SCPMG physician, still practicing
journey.fortune_basis: so I have the longest tenure now
journey.quote: I'm the longest standing physician in Southern California. Permanente no one joined before July 1st, 1969 is still working.

events.name: Permanente Federation founded
events.view: He counts helping bring the Permanente Medical Groups together in the Federation as what he was most proud of.
events.quote: I was most proud of taking the lead on bringing the Permanente Medical Groups together in the Federation.

prompt.question: What were you most proud of during your tenure as MD?

events.name: Electronic health record rollout

events.quote: Along came George Halvorson, as the president of the health plan, chief executive out of Minnesota. And, uh, George, uh, his unique contribution was to expose all of us

prompt.question: Do you want to talk about, you know, because you were there when we decided you worked with Halvorson to decide on epic, right?

events.name: Hospital closure plan
events.view: He inherited a plan to close some Kaiser hospitals, cooperated while doubting it, and later called his support a mistake.
events.quote: I stepped into my position in leadership when the decision had been made to try to close some Kaiser hospitals. It sounded wrong, but it was already made.

prompt.question: Can you tell us your thinking process that allowed you to change your opinion on closing hospitals and keeping them?

events.name: 1990s financial crisis
events.view: He saw the health plan's losses after a premium reduction as a crisis he had warned about, threatening physicians' incomes.
events.quote: Then the financial crisis came when we began to lose hundreds of millions of dollars

prompt.question: the question was the greatest challenges that you experienced as a leader. So what? What event?

events.name: Managed care competition
events.view: He saw managed care competitors as a threat to membership that SCPMG prevailed over during his tenure.
events.quote: Managed care said we're going to eat Kaiser Permanente's lunch.

prompt.question: the question was the greatest challenges that you experienced as a leader. So what? What event?

events.name: Tahoe agreement
events.view: He named Tahoe I as a pivotal moment in which the health plan and medical group set direction together.
events.quote: The pivotal issues between the health plan and medical group, we call it Tahoe I, uh, and setting the direction together and what we're going to do

prompt.question: can you describe a pivotal moment in the history of Kaiser Permanente that has shaped its current practices?

events.name: HIV/AIDS epidemic
events.view: He saw KP's quick build-up of specialized HIV clinics and training as an example of the organization embracing a new disease.
events.quote: Let me give you an example of HIV. HIV disease was not understood at the beginning.

prompt.question: how did Kaiser Permanente during those years adapt to changes in healthcare, you know, like governmental rules, healthcare, different things that happen during your years.

events.name: COVID-19 pandemic
events.view: Practicing after his term, he was impressed by how fast KP set up vaccination centers and vaccinated patients.
events.quote: we embraced the idea of the immunization. Swiftly, new clinics arose, new Covid vaccination centers. It was astonishing how fast we got everybody who we could get vaccinated for Covid

prompt.question: how did Kaiser Permanente during those years adapt to changes in healthcare, you know, like governmental rules, healthcare, different things that happen during your years.

events.name: Member assessment of physician services (MAPS)
events.view: He pushed for patient ratings of physicians over pay-based arguments and is proud the measure he designed later rated him.
events.quote: Let's do maps. And since then, 1999, maybe 2000, we assess our physicians by membership, uh, assessments.

prompt.question: Can you share an example of a successful project or program you led at Kaiser Permanente?

events.name: KP National Diversity program
events.view: He was the first Permanente co-leader of the health plan's national diversity group and tied a diverse workforce to patient compliance.
events.quote: So I was the national Permanente representative, first one ever in our program, to the National Diversity Group that came out of the health plan.

prompt.question: What initiatives, um, did you do to promote diversity and inclusion within Kaiser Permanente?

events.name: Kaiser Permanente School of Medicine opened
events.view: He saw his era's scholarships and research hires as preliminary steps toward the medical school KP eventually opened.
events.quote: Ultimately, we we we opened, as you know, the medical school to advance our science.

prompt.question: How does Kaiser Permanente support research and development in medical science?

retellable.title: The pre-op potassium audit
retellable.summary: As quality committee chair, he wrote an audit the anesthesiology chief said was unnecessary, checking potassium before every surgery. It found unnoticed low potassium causing arrhythmias, and pre-op potassium checks became routine.
retellable.quote: Let's do a pre-op potassium on every patient going to surgery. And lo and behold, we found that there were complications, arrhythmias in patients who had low K's and it wasn't being found.
retellable.why: Simple quality audit that changed surgical practice and saved money

retellable.title: Owning a public mistake
retellable.summary: He publicly endorsed moving the cardiac surgery program from Kaiser Sunset, and the plan failed immediately. He told the medical group it was his mistake and was re-elected two years later.
retellable.quote: Success has many parents okay; this one was failure. Oliver's the parent. Well, another characteristic of leadership is candor. I made the mistake. Stop there. I, Oliver, your leader, made this mistake.
retellable.why: A leader's candid account of admitting error and keeping trust

retellable.title: Who designed this thing? It was me
retellable.summary: He championed patient assessments of physicians (MAPS) against a board member who argued for paying doctors more. Back in practice later, he found himself rated by the system he had designed.
retellable.quote: it was humorous for me when I went back into practice, I began to get these assessments, and I made a lighthearted comment, who designed this thing? My patients are are evaluating me. It was me.
retellable.why: Humorous origin story for patient-measured physician quality

retellable.title: Edgar Kaiser and the bauxite
retellable.summary: Called to treat Edgar Kaiser, he hospitalized him at Kaiser Sunset and waited while Kaiser finished a call to Jamaica. Not knowing what bauxite was, he offered to order it.
retellable.quote: I'm on the phone to Jamaica. I said, Jamaica. He said, you know, bauxite and I, I didn't know and I said, bauxite. I got mixed up. I said, well, I think I can order that if you need it.
retellable.why: Warm, funny first-hand encounter with Edgar Kaiser as a patient
